column1: A person carries a bag at constant height while walking horizontally. How much work does gravity do on the bag?
column2: Zero — gravity is vertical, displacement is horizontal, so θ=90° and cos(90°)=0.

column1: A ball moves in a circle at constant speed on a string. How much work does the tension (centripetal force) do?
column2: Zero — tension is always perpendicular to velocity/displacement, which is exactly why speed (and KE) stays constant.

column1: Is gravitational potential energy an absolute value or relative to something?
column2: Relative — PE = mgh depends on your chosen reference height. Only CHANGES in PE are physically meaningful.

column1: A box slides across a rough floor and stops. What equation correctly applies conservation of energy?
column2: KE<sub>i</sub> + PE<sub>i</sub> = KE<sub>f</sub> + PE<sub>f</sub> + W<sub>friction</sub> — you must add the energy lost to friction, not assume simple conservation.

column1: If you double the compression distance x of a spring, how does its elastic PE change?
column2: It quadruples — PE<sub>spring</sub> = ½kx² is quadratic in x.

column1: Two people carry the same box up the same stairs (same height gained), but one takes half the time. Compare their work and power.
column2: Same work (same force, same displacement) — but the faster person has GREATER power (same energy delivered in less time).
W<sub>net</sub> = ΔKE — the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.

column1: What is the formula for work?
column2: W = Fd·cos(θ) — only the force component parallel to displacement does work.

column1: What is the formula for kinetic energy?
When is total mechanical energy (KE+PE) conserved?
column2: When only conservative forces (gravity, springs) act — no friction or air resistance.
P = W/t = Fv — the RATE of doing work / transferring energy (Watts), not a total amount (Joules).

column1: Name common forces that do ZERO work on an object, and why.
column2: Normal force, and tension/centripetal force in circular motion — all act perpendicular to the direction of motion.
